newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Central banker seeks balance on Taiwan stock rally.
newsitem.headline: Central banker seeks balance on Taiwan stock rally.

text.p: Taiwan's central banker said on Thursday he was "a bit worried" about the island's surging stock market, but not enough to order measures to tighten loose liquidity in the money market.
"The central bank is a bit worried about the recent stock market rally," central bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong told parliament in comments about the bank's fiscal policy.
Sheu reiterated the central bank's intention to lower banks' reserve requirements at the "appropriate" time, but gave no timetable.
"Taiwan's reserve requirements compared with other countries are a little bit too high," Sheu said. "The central bank will lower them at an appropriate time, but not now.

Sheu pledged to maintain the bank's longstanding "stable to loose" monetary policy, which aims to keep enough liquidity in circulation to ensure Taiwan's slowly accelerating recovery reaches its full potential without reigniting inflation.
Despite unexepectedly low consumer price increases in January and February, Sheu cautioned that he remained worried about inflation in some unspecified economic sectors.
"The central bank will continue our stable to loose policy, but not too loose because of worries about inflation in certain sectors," he said.

Sheu described the stock market's dramatic 75-80 percent rise since March 1996 as acceptable, noting that that even at current levels above 8,000 points the main index remains far below a frothy historic peak of more than 12,600 hit in 1990.
"The recent stock market rise shows that the market simply has returned to normal because it plunged too much in the past," Sheu said, referring to a late 1990 plunge below 2,500.

The index, which has gained more than 1,000 points in 1997 alone, jumped 1.32 percent in early trading, buoyed chiefly by Wall Street's overnight rise, and was holding onto most of those gains as Sheu continued to address parliament.

Some economists, including some of Sheu's central bank deputies, have voiced concern that the big market rise was being fuelled largely by loose liquidity under the bank's monetary policy, rather than reflecting fundamental equity value.
Sheu vowed to maintain a hands-off stock market policy.
"The share values should be determined by investors in the market," he said.
Sheu also pledged to refrain as much as possible from making further comment about the rallying market. "We make as little comment as possible on the stock market," he said.
